category_title: Middle school students who disengage and use ritualistic rule-following when encountering fractions
minimal_context: The student is sitting one-on-one with an interviewer and working on paper to solve the arithmetic exercise 2/3 * 9.
dialogue:
TUTOR: Please solve this arithmetic exercise on the paper: 2/3 * 9.

STUDENT: (Looks at paper) Now, here I'll put two thirds times nine and I'll make from it one thing so it will be easier for me... So, here I'll write... I'll do like this, two times nine divided by three times one. (Looks at interviewer) Is it right to do like that?

TUTOR: What do you think you should do next?

STUDENT: (Quietly, biting lip, looking down) With fractions I'm not good so I don't know... (Looks up at interviewer, raised, contracted eyebrows, slightly anxious expression) Maybe by half?

TUTOR: Just keep trying to solve it.

STUDENT: (Thinks) It can be simplified. (Erases what she has written) Because I have to solve the exercise from the beginning... I simplify the nine and then I'll get three and one.

options.A: Tend to the gaps in the student's mathematical knowledge hierarchy and include parents to shift evaluation criteria from grades to understanding.
options.B: Provide the student with access to similar, but more socially appropriate, sensory stimulation by giving her a squishy, stress-relief ball.
options.C: Maintain a quiet and relaxing environment during the interview, talking gently and slowly to the student while avoiding any loud speech.
options.D: Radically remove time constraints during the interview, slowing down the pace of the arithmetic exercises as much as required by the student.
